title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3
description: Trace the evolution of HTTP and understand how each version changed web performance.

data.text: HTTP is the protocol of the web. Every website, API call, and image download travels over HTTP. Since 1991, it has evolved from a simple document-fetching protocol into a binary, multiplexed transport that powers modern single-page applications and microservices.

Each major version of HTTP solved a specific bottleneck. HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and caching. HTTP/2 added binary framing and multiplexing. HTTP/3 replaced TCP with QUIC to eliminate head-of-line blocking at the transport layer.
HTTP/1.1: The Era of Text and Connections

HTTP/1.1, standardized in 1997, is still widely used. It is human-readable, stateless, and built on plain-text requests and responses. Browsers open multiple TCP connections to work around its limitation: only one request per connection at a time.

data.title: HTTP/1.1 Features
items: Persistent connections — reuse a single TCP connection for multiple requests.
Chunked transfer encoding — send data in chunks without knowing the total size upfront.
Cache controls — headers like ETag and Cache-Control let servers and browsers skip redundant downloads.
Content negotiation — servers can return different representations based on Accept headers.

data.title: Head-of-Line Blocking
data.text: If a large image is downloading on one HTTP/1.1 connection, a smaller CSS file behind it must wait. Browsers open 6 to 8 connections per domain, but this still wastes resources and adds latency.

HTTP/2, published in 2015, is a complete rewrite of the wire format. It replaces text-based messages with binary frames and lets multiple requests and responses travel on a single TCP connection simultaneously. This is called multiplexing.

data.title: HTTP/2 Improvements
items: Multiplexing — send many requests in parallel over one connection.
Header compression — HPACK reduces redundant header overhead.
Server push — servers can send resources before the browser asks.
Stream prioritization — browsers can tell the server which resources matter most.

data.text: HTTP/3, standardized in 2022, drops TCP entirely. It runs over QUIC, a transport protocol built on UDP. QUIC eliminates head-of-line blocking because a lost packet only blocks the stream that used it, not every stream on the connection.

QUIC also combines the TLS handshake with the connection setup. In HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, establishing a secure connection requires a TCP handshake plus a TLS handshake — two round trips. QUIC does both in one, which noticeably speeds up page loads on high-latency networks like mobile.

cards.title: HTTP/1.1
cards.description: Text-based, one request per connection, simple and universal.
pros: Simple to debug with telnet or netcat

cards.title: HTTP/2
cards.description: Binary framing, multiplexed streams, header compression.
cons: Still suffers from TCP head-of-line blocking

cards.title: HTTP/3
cards.description: QUIC over UDP, eliminates transport-layer blocking.
pros: Better performance on mobile and lossy networks
cons: UDP may be blocked by some middleboxes
Newer ecosystem with fewer debugging tools
QUIC is more complex to implement

data.title: Real-World Adoption
data.text: As of 2024, over 30% of the top one million websites serve HTTP/3. Cloudflare, Google, and Facebook have all adopted it broadly. For new projects, enabling HTTP/3 through a CDN is often a single configuration change.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and caching but suffered from head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/2 added binary framing, multiplexing, and header compression.
HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC to remove transport-layer blocking and speed up handshakes.
Choosing the right version depends on your users, your infrastructure, and how modern your tooling is.
data.takeaway: HTTP evolution is a masterclass in how protocols optimize for real-world bottlenecks: latency, bandwidth, and packet loss.
